summary: Describes mechanisms for giving TRILL edge switches directory information. The information can reduce flooding of multi-destination traffic, such as ARP, Neighbor Discovery and unknown unicast. It can also help detect forged source addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of shouting in a crowded room to find someone, you check a list that says where each person sits.

what is a pull directory query
subtitle: How TRILL switches look up where an address lives instead of flooding the whole network to find out.

tldr.problem: In a TRILL campus, ARP, Neighbor Discovery and frames to unknown unicast destinations are flooded to many switches, which becomes a burden as the network grows.
tldr.mechanism: Directory servers hold address mapping data. A Push Directory sends it to interested switches through ESADI, and a Pull Directory answers queries carried in RBridge Channel messages.
tldr.outcome: Edge switches can answer ARP/ND locally, unicast instead of flood, and detect forged source addresses. This is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8171 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2017. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs Directories
sections.content:
A TRILL campus normally floods multi-destination traffic such as ARP, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) and frames with an unknown unicast destination. RFC 7067 gave the problem statement and high-level design for using directory servers to cut this traffic and to improve security against address spoofing. RFC 8171 specifies the actual mechanisms.

The directory holds address mapping and reachability information. The most common case is which MAC address matches an IP address within a Data Label (a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label), which egress TRILL switch (RBridge) it is reachable from and, optionally, which port. How a primary server first gets its data is out of scope. In a data center, orchestration software that already knows where every address and VLAN is can supply it.

An edge switch that has directory information can intercept ARP and ND requests and reply itself, can unicast a frame whose destination it knows instead of flooding it, and, with complete directory data, can discard frames with a forged source MAC or IP address. Directory services come in a Push mode, a Pull mode, or both, at the discretion of the server.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer wants to find another one, it normally yells to everybody. A directory is a phone book, so the network can look the answer up instead of yelling.

sections.title: The Push Model
sections.content:
In the Push Model, one or more Push Directory servers on TRILL switches "push down" address mapping data for a Data Label. The data is distributed with the ESADI protocol (RFC 7357). A switch subscribes simply by announcing, in its IS-IS link state PDUs, the Data Labels for which it takes part in ESADI.

A server advertises that it is available by setting the Push Directory Server Status (PDSS) field of its ESADI-Parameter APPsub-TLV to a non-zero value. Each server is configured with a number N from 1 to 8 (default 2) of copies to push, and with an 8-bit priority PushDirPriority that defaults to 0x3F. Ties go to the larger System ID. A server ranks the reachable servers for the Data Label and finds its position K. If K is at most N it is Active, otherwise it is Stand-By.

A receiving switch can only get reasonable assurance, not certainty, that its data is complete. It needs the server to advertise PDSS 3 and to have had continuous connectivity to it for a configurable time that defaults to twice the server's CSNP time. If a Push Directory server stops being data reachable, other switches MUST ignore its data. When sources conflict, higher confidence wins; on equal confidence Push Directory data beats locally learned data, and a higher-priority server beats a lower one.

A secondary server can obtain its data from a primary server by default through the Push mechanism. It is RECOMMENDED that re-originated data get a confidence level at least one lower.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book company mails updated pages to everyone who signed up. You do not have to ask, but you must trust that the pages are current.

sections.title: Push Directory Server States
sections.content:
For each Data Label it serves, a Push Directory server is in one of seven states. The state decides the PDSS value it advertises.

  • Down (PDSS 0): shut down, nothing advertised.
  • Stand-By (PDSS 1): participates in ESADI but advertises no directory data.
  • Active (PDSS 2): advertises directory data and updates.
  • Active Completing (PDSS 2): behaves like Active while waiting long enough for data to reach subscribers before claiming completeness.
  • Active Complete (PDSS 3): has pushed complete data.
  • Going Stand-By Was Complete and Active Uncompleting (both PDSS 2): transition states that give the news that the directory is no longer complete time to propagate before updates stop.

Seven events drive the transitions, including the server coming up, being shut down, meeting the Activate or Stand-By Condition (with or without a configuration saying the data is complete), a change to configuration saying the data is not complete, and the Time Condition, which is being in the current state for PushDirTimer (default twice the CSNP time).

The extra transition states exist for a reason. If a complete directory went straight to Active and then immediately to Stand-By, it could stop advertising updates before every edge switch had learned it was incomplete.
sections.plainLanguage: A server does not just say "my list is finished" the moment it sends the last page. It waits a bit so everyone has really received it, and waits again before saying "not finished" so nobody is misled.

sections.title: Pull Directory Messages
sections.content:
In the Pull Model a switch asks a directory server when it needs information. Servers for a Data Label are found in the IS-IS link state database by looking for data-reachable switches that set the PUL flag in their Interested VLANs or Interested Labels sub-TLV. Requests go in RBridge Channel messages (RFC 7178) using a Pull Directory channel protocol number. Queries are normally derived from ingressed ARP, ND, RARP or SEND messages, or from frames with unknown unicast destinations.

All messages share an 8-byte header: Ver, Type, Flags, Count, Err, SubErr and a 32-bit Sequence Number. Types are 1 Query, 2 Response, 3 Update and 4 Acknowledge. A Query holds zero or more QUERY records; a Count of 0 is allowed as a ping. QTYPE 1 asks for the addresses of an interface given one address. QTYPE 2 and 5 carry a whole frame (an ARP, ND, RARP, or unknown-unicast frame), and the server can answer it itself or forward it.

A Response carries RESPONSE records, each with a Lifetime in units of 100 milliseconds. Zero means the answer must not be cached, and 2**16 - 1 means it may be kept until the server goes away. Positive and negative answers are both RECOMMENDED to be cached, and the timer is not extended when an entry is used. If a query gets no answer in DirQueryTimeout (default 100 milliseconds), it is retransmitted up to DirQueryRetries times (default 3).

Errors are a two-part Err and SubErr code. Err 1 to 126 are message-level errors and 128 to 254 are record-level errors, such as 130 for Address not found.
sections.plainLanguage: When you do not have the page you need, you send a note asking the phone book desk. The desk replies with the answer and tells you how long you can trust it.

sections.title: Keeping Caches Consistent
sections.content:
Unless it only sends answers with Lifetime 0, a Pull Directory server MUST take action to limit how long a switch keeps stale data. It does this with Update messages and chooses one of three record-keeping methods. Method 1 is the least specific: it remembers only when the last positive and negative answers per Data Label expire. Method 2 tracks each unit of data and negative answer. Method 3 tracks which switches were told what. A server MUST support method 1 and SHOULD support methods 2 and 3, and it moves to a lower-numbered method if it hits its limits.

The Flags field of an Update has bits F (flood), P (positive) and N (negative). With method 1, a flush is flooded with Count 0 meaning all addresses. With methods 2 and 3, a message has either P or N set, but not both. Method 3 normally unicasts updates only to the switches that may hold the data. Updates are sent with priority DirUpdatePriority, default 5, and may be delayed by DirUpdateDelay (default 50 milliseconds) to batch changes.

Clients answer with Acknowledge messages. Finally, a client MUST be able to tell when a server is no longer reachable and MUST promptly discard everything it cached from it, because it can no longer receive updates.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone book changes, the desk sends a note to people who copied the old page. Some desks keep careful lists of who has which page, and some just tell everybody to throw their copy away.

sections.title: Hybrid Use and End Stations
sections.content:
Push and Pull can be mixed. A data-center gateway that talks to many Data Labels may have pushed mappings for the VLANs it uses all the time (the RFC's example is VLANs 1 through 100) and pull the rest on demand. Within one Data Label, commonly referenced addresses such as gateways and DNS or database servers can be pushed as an incomplete directory while others are pulled. The operator decides this by configuration. All switches SHOULD have a strategy for the period when their directory data is not yet complete, such as sending a Pull query or reverting to base TRILL behavior.

When a switch needs data for a frame, it can flood immediately, flood after a delay, or discard. The RFC gives a recommended mapping from the frame's priority to the priority of the query.

End stations are supported through TRILL ES-IS, a variation of TRILL IS-IS for links with both switches and end stations. It lets an end station host a Pull Directory, which an RBridge then fronts for the rest of the campus, or use a Pull Directory from its edge RBridge. End stations use port MAC addresses in place of System IDs. Directory servers that do not want multi-destination traffic can set the No Data (NOD) bit, but a Push Directory MUST NOT set it if it needs multi-destination ESADI or Channel PDUs in that Data Label.
sections.plainLanguage: For the names you look up all the time, keep a copy at hand. For rarely needed ones, ask when you need them. Both work together.

sections.title: Security and IANA Actions
sections.content:
Incorrect directory data can deliver traffic to the wrong end stations, or cause denial of service through black holes or by discarding frames based on wrong information. So directory data must be protected from unauthorized modification, and servers need access control that is not overly permissive. Anyone allowed to read the data can violate privacy policies, though RBridges already see plain-text ARP, ND and IP traffic.

Push Directory data travels in ESADI-LSPs, so the widely deployed IS-IS PDU authentication gives it authentication and integrity protection. Pull messages are RBridge Channel messages and can be secured with the mechanisms in RFC 7978, which can add confidentiality, though the RFC says these were believed to be less widely implemented than IS-IS security.

IANA assigned RBridge Channel protocol number 0x005 for Pull Directory Services, assigned the PUL and NOD flag bits, and created registries for Pull Directory query types and error codes.
sections.plainLanguage: A wrong phone book sends people to the wrong house, so only trusted people should be allowed to write in it.
